content_voiceover: Waldenström macroglobulinemia is driven by clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells that secrete monoclonal IgM, and its clinical picture flows directly from that biology. In the bone marrow, infiltration causes cytopenias in a characteristic order of severity, hemoglobin drops the most, platelets somewhat less, and white count least of all. The IgM paraprotein itself is directly responsible for hyperviscosity syndrome, presenting with epistaxis, headaches, and impaired vision, and this typically becomes clinically significant once IgM exceeds about six thousand milligrams per deciliter or serum viscosity rises above four centipoise, both classic board thresholds to remember. Marrow involvement can also drive up hepcidin, which restricts iron availability and contributes to an anemia of inflammation on top of the marrow replacement anemia. Beyond hyperviscosity, IgM causes several other named complications, cold agglutinin disease in about five percent, cryoglobulinemia in about ten percent, IgM-related peripheral neuropathy in about twenty two percent, and amyloidosis in ten to fifteen percent. A distinctive neurologic complication is Bing-Neel syndrome, direct central nervous system infiltration by lymphoplasmacytic cells. Lymphadenopathy is present in only about twenty percent of patients at diagnosis but becomes much more common, fifty to sixty percent, at relapse.
keypoints: Marrow infiltration: Hb drops most, then platelets, then WBC
Hyperviscosity from IgM causes epistaxis, headache, vision changes, typically IgM over 6000 or CP over 4.0
IgM complications: cold agglutinin 5 percent, cryoglobulinemia 10 percent, neuropathy 22 percent, amyloidosis 10-15 percent
Bing-Neel syndrome is CNS infiltration; lymphadenopathy rises from 20 percent at diagnosis to 50-60 percent at relapse
keypoint_voiceover: Focus on the hyperviscosity thresholds, the spectrum of IgM-mediated complications including neuropathy and amyloidosis, and Bing-Neel syndrome as the CNS variant of this disease.
